The first assignment

Monday, 7 September, nine o’clock, a photo agency in Malasaña, Madrid. It’s Andrei’s first day as an intern. His boss, Begoña Arrieta, used to be a war photographer. His colleague, Lucas, is from Cádiz.
When I saw you come in, I thought you were a lost student. Are you the Romanian with the photo from the fair?
Yes. I arrived last Monday. As soon as I’d dropped off my bags, I went out to take photos.
Good. Here we don’t wait for permission. As soon as you see something, you shoot.
And before you forget: the coffee from the machine is horrible. There’s a bar downstairs.
Your first assignment: old bookshops in Madrid that are still open. Bookshops that hold out. I want a series by the end of the month.
For what day exactly?
For the 28th. Once you have twenty good photos, show them to me. Not one before.
I know a place that isn’t a bookshop any more, but still has its light on.
Tell me about it when you finish the series. As you get to know the city, you’ll see that all Madrid’s stories begin in a bar or in a bookshop.
Or in both at once. Once the meeting’s over, I’ll buy you that coffee. Welcome, Romanian.

“al” links to the verb like an extra syllable: [al-ver-TE], [al-lle-GAR]. Don’t pause after “al”.
The “n” of “en” assimilates to the “c”: it sounds almost like [eŋ-KUAN-to], like the “n” in English “anchor”.
Stress on “di”: [a-me-DI-da-ke]. The “d” between vowels is soft, almost like the “th” in English “this”.
1. Al + infinitive and nada más + infinitive
When I saw you come in, I thought you were a student.
When I came out of the metro, it started to rain.
As soon as I arrived, my mother called me.
“Al + infinitive” = at the same moment (when). “Nada más + infinitive” = immediately after. Both are invariable: you don’t conjugate the verb; the subject is understood from the context.
2. En cuanto, tan pronto como, una vez que, a medida que
Indicative (habits, past)
Subjunctive (future)
en cuanto / tan pronto como
En cuanto llego, me ducho.

una vez que

a medida que
A medida que pasaban los días, se sentía mejor.
A medida que conozcas la ciudad, te gustará más.
The B1 rule still applies: when the action is in the future, the time connector is followed by the SUBJUNCTIVE, never the future: «En cuanto llegue» ✓, «En cuanto llegaré» ✗.
3. Desde que, hasta que, antes de que
Since he arrived in Madrid, he hasn’t got lost even once.
He didn’t stop until he understood the weather forecast.
I won’t stop until I understand it.
Before you forget, write down the address.
“Antes de que” ALWAYS takes the subjunctive, even in the past: «Se fue antes de que yo llegara». If the subject is the same, use “antes de + infinitive”: «Antes de salir, apaga la luz».
4. The absolute participle
In careful language, an agreeing participle at the start of the sentence replaces a whole time clause:
Once the meeting was over, we went for a coffee.
Once the photos were published, the café filled up with people.
That said, he got up and left.
The participle agrees with the noun that follows it: terminadA la reunión, publicadAS las fotos, terminadOS los exámenes.

Septiembre en Madrid

On his first morning in the calle del Prado, Andrei woke at six, long before the alarm went off. Marta was still asleep. He made coffee in an Italian coffee pot he didn’t know how to use, couldn’t find the sugar and drank it bitter, standing in the hallway in front of the green sign. As soon as he had finished his coffee, he picked up his camera and went out. Madrid was empty, freshly hosed down, and smelt of bread and bleach.

Without thinking much about it, his feet took him to the Retiro. When he reached the lake, he looked for the bench where Ecaterina had recited the Machado poem in May. It was empty, wet from the sprinklers, with a dry leaf on it. He took a single photo. Then he wrote to Ecaterina: “I’m sending you the bench. This morning nobody skipped a line.” She answered a minute later, although it was eight o’clock in Bucharest: “Thank you. Now go to work.”

The first week he got lost every day. He took the wrong metro line, got off at stations named after saints he’d never heard of and once ended up on an industrial estate on the outskirts, photographing cranes. But he also discovered that Madrid was full of Romanians. The lady at the kiosk in the plaza de Santa Ana was from Iași; the waiter at the bar downstairs, from Craiova; and the man who repaired bicycles on the corner, from a village near Suceava with the same name as his grandmother’s.

On Thursday he went to see Lola. As he walked into El Mostrador, she recognised the embroidered camera strap at once and came out from behind the bar to hug him. The café was full: people were reading at every table, and on the shelves the books from the funeral now had little coloured slips of paper peeping out from between the pages. Lola showed him a notebook she had left by the till, where customers wrote down what they had found inside the borrowed books: a cinema ticket from 1979, a recipe for croquetas, an unsigned declaration of love.

On Monday 7 September he started at the agency. It was on a third floor with no lift in Malasaña, its walls covered in framed photos: wars, football matches, royal weddings, demonstrations, fires. The boss, Begoña Arrieta, was a Basque woman of about sixty, with very short grey hair and a voice that didn’t need to be raised to make itself heard. She had spent twenty years photographing wars. Since she had come back, she said, she only photographed things that didn’t explode.

The colleague at the next desk was called Lucas. He was from Cádiz, twenty-eight years old, talked at a speed Andrei took two weeks to keep up with and swallowed half his consonants. On the first day he explained three essential things: that the coffee from the machine was horrible, that Begoña never said a photo was good, only that it “wasn’t bad”, and that if she ever said “not bad”, it had to be celebrated. In two years, she had said it to him four times.

Begoña’s first lesson was a strange one. She asked for his digital camera, locked it in a drawer and gave him an old film camera instead, with thirty-six exposures. She told him she wouldn’t give him the digital one back until he had learnt to wait. It took Andrei five days to use up the roll. For the first time in his life, before pressing the button, he stood looking, counted to ten and asked himself whether that photo was worth it. Of the thirty-six, Begoña saved only two. But she gave him back the digital camera.

The first assignment was a series about old bookshops in Madrid that were still open. Begoña called it “Bookshops that hold out”. Andrei made a list that very night: he found thirty-four bookshops more than fifty years old. Begoña crossed out twenty-four without explaining why and told him ten would be more than enough. She gave him until the 28th. And she warned him that once he had twenty good photos, he should show them to her; not one before.

He started with the Cuesta de Moyano, next to the Retiro, where a row of wooden stalls has sold second-hand books for almost a hundred years. As he approached the last stall, a very old man in a beret and a scarf in the middle of September asked him what he was looking for. Andrei told him about the series. The man was called Faustino and he was eighty-seven. When Andrei mentioned calle de las Huertas, Faustino took off his beret. “Gil? The La Lámpara one?” he said. “That man used to steal my customers. He was the best bookseller in Madrid.”

Faustino took a shoebox full of photos out from under the counter. He went through them slowly, with crooked fingers, until he found the one he was looking for. It was from 1985. It showed Andrés, still young, in a corduroy jacket, in front of the green sign. Beside him, a woman with long hair was laughing with her head thrown back, as if she had just been told the best joke in the world. Faustino said he had taken the photo himself, one Sunday morning. “Give it to the lady,” he said. “It’s no use to me any more, but it is to her.”

Before they said goodbye, Faustino asked him whether it was true about the plaque. Andrei told him yes, it would be unveiled on 7 October, at midday. The old bookseller thought for a moment, put his beret back on and said he would go, even if he had to close the stall, something he hadn’t done since his wife’s funeral. He said he would wear his best beret. Andrei didn’t dare ask how many he had.

Andrei took a photo of the photo and sent it to Ecaterina as soon as he left the stall. She took an hour to reply. When she did, she wrote: “That photo is from the day he asked me to marry him for the second time. I said no. I’m laughing because I couldn’t believe it: he asked me in front of the whole Cuesta de Moyano, shouting, and Faustino was there with his camera.” Then she added: “Tell Faustino I still owe him for a Neruda book. I’ll pay him in October.”

In Bucharest, Ecaterina wrote every morning from six until the sun reached the table. On 12 September she had a video call with Marta’s editor, a woman from Barcelona called Inés Vidal, who talked very fast and laughed even faster. When the call ended, Inés sent her a contract. Ecaterina, who had translated hundreds of contracts at the trade office, took three days to read it, line by line, with a red pencil. As soon as she had finished, she signed it without changing a single comma.

That month she was writing the hardest chapter: the night of 23 February 1981, in the bookshop, with the radio on and the fear of not knowing what country they would wake up to. It took her twelve mornings to write. Once it was finished, she read it aloud to Rosa Elena, who understood almost nothing because it was in Spanish. Even so, the little girl listened to the end without moving and then said it was very beautiful, but a bit sad. Ecaterina thought it was the best review she could get.

On 15 September, Rosa Elena started her last year of kindergarten. She turned up on the first day with the camera Andrei had given her hanging round her neck and, before the teacher could say anything, took her photo. The teacher asked whose camera it was. Rosa Elena explained that it was hers, that she was a photographer and that, besides, she was going to be a lorry driver and a translator, but that would be later, when she finished kindergarten.

Costel, meanwhile, was counting the days left until the exam. On Thursdays, Ana gave him practice exams at the kitchen table, with a stopwatch. In written expression he was already getting 71. His problem was listening comprehension: the Andalusians in the recordings spoke as fast as Lucas. So he had set himself a rule: he would listen to Spanish radio in the cab every day until he understood the whole weather forecast, without missing a word.

On top of that, from Valencia, his grandson Álex tested him on the phone every Wednesday. He was a teenager and asked him about the expressions his friends at school used, which didn’t appear in any textbook. Costel wrote words like “flipar”, “renta” or “literal” in his notebook and repeated them in the cab until he had learnt them. Ana warned him they would be no use at all in the exam. Costel replied that the exam lasted four hours, but his grandson would last him a lifetime.

The evenings were the hardest part. When he got home, Andrei found the flat silent and Marta writing in the living room with her headphones on. At first they ate dinner in their own rooms, out of shyness. But one night the power went off in the whole building, and they had to eat together in the kitchen, by candlelight: bread with tomato and a tin of sardines. They talked until two. From that night on they always ate together, even when there was power.

Carmen kept Ana’s promise: she called every Sunday at ten. On the second Sunday she didn’t call; she turned up in person, with a tub of lentils the size of a suitcase. Juan waited in the car, double-parked. Carmen told Andrei she wouldn’t leave until he had eaten a plateful in front of her. Andrei ate it. Then she gave him five more tubs for the week, with the days written on the lids in marker pen.

As the days went by, Andrei began to see the city instead of looking at it. He photographed a bookshop on calle del Pez where the owner took his siesta among the shelves; another in Lavapiés, tiny, run by two seventy-year-old twin sisters who never agreed on anything; and a second-hand bookshop in Chamberí where a grey cat always slept on top of the complete works of Galdós and nobody dared move it.

The twin sisters in Lavapiés gave him more work than all the others put together. They couldn’t agree on the year they had opened the bookshop: one said 1962 and the other 1963, and they had been arguing about it for sixty years. Before Andrei could take the first photo, they asked him to decide. Andrei searched the back room until he found an old, yellowed invoice dated 4 January 1963. The sister who had said 1963 talked about nothing else all afternoon.

At the end of the month he received his first salary. It wasn’t much, but it was the first. With part of it he bought his father a book about the historic bridges of Madrid. Then he got up at six, went to the Toledo bridge over the river Manzanares and waited until the sun came up. He sent the photo to his father. Señor Dan replied with a technical comment about the eighteenth-century granite arches. An hour later he sent another, shorter message: “And the photo, too.”

He took the missing photo one rainy night, at two in the morning. He walked to calle de las Huertas with an umbrella that was no use at all. El Mostrador was closed, with the chairs upside down on the tables. But at the back, where the real counter used to be, the lamp was still on, as Lola had promised. Through the wet glass, the light seemed to tremble. Andrei waited until a man walked past with a dog, so the street wouldn’t be empty. He took a single photo.

On 28 September, at nine sharp, he showed Begoña twenty printed photos. She looked at them in silence, one by one, without saying anything, for a quarter of an hour. Lucas, at his desk, pretended to work. When she reached the photo of the lamp, Begoña stopped. She asked him what that place was. Andrei told her the whole story: the bookseller, the translator, the letters, the funeral, Lola’s promise. It took him twenty minutes. Begoña didn’t interrupt him once.

When he had finished, Begoña put the photo down on the table and said: “Not bad.” Lucas jumped up from his chair as if he had been stung. Begoña explained to Andrei that the series would be published in a newspaper’s Sunday supplement on 5 October, and that this photo would open it, full page. Then she added something Andrei wrote down in his notebook that same night: “A good photo isn’t taken when you see something, but when you understand it. It took you a month to understand this one. That’s not long.”

Once the meeting was over, Lucas took him to the bar downstairs and ordered two small beers and a plate of calamari to celebrate. He told him that the first time Begoña said “not bad” to him, he called his mother in Cádiz, and his mother threw a barbecue for the whole neighbourhood. Andrei called Ecaterina. He told her about the photo, the supplement, the “not bad”. Ecaterina was silent for a moment. Then she said: “In the end, Andrés was right. The light stays on. And someone sees it.”

In Bucharest, meanwhile, the club was already preparing for the October trip. Ana and Mihai had bought the tickets as soon as they heard the date. Ecaterina would travel with them. Costel had asked his boss for three days off, although the exam was getting closer and closer, and had said he would study on the plane. Mrs Florica, who had never been on a plane, had announced that she was coming too, because someone had to take Andrei some proper food, and because, according to her, a plaque like that isn’t unveiled every day.

On the evening of 30 September, Andrei went out onto the balcony of the flat on the calle del Prado. It had been a month since he arrived. He realised that this week he hadn’t got lost even once, that the waiter downstairs now served his coffee without asking and that he dreamt in Spanish at least one night in three. He wrote a single sentence in the club’s group chat: “September: done.” Before he could put his phone away, Costel had already replied: “October: we’re all coming.”
